32: Since doorstep visitors stay only briefly and appear at random times, and residents cannot always answer the door immediately, the need to see who is at the door, keep records, and remotely handle situations when necessary has become a clear practical requirement. Therefore, this project naturally presents a complete design of a Raspberry Pi based smart doorbell system with facial recognition: the device side performs camera frame capture and local recognition, the cloud side handles data management and command scheduling, and the Android client is used for viewing and remote control.
33: The overall system reasonably adopts a three-tier collaborative architecture comprising device-side local recognition, cloud-side centralized management, and mobile-side remote control. The device side takes a video stream as input, uses dlib (face_recognition) for face detection and feature extraction, then performs distance comparison against a local member feature database. When a member is recognized, it triggers a buzzer alert and door lock linkage (simulated by a stepper motor), while employing an action cooldown window to prevent repeated triggering. When an unknown visitor is recognized, it automatically captures a snapshot for record keeping, and enters an alert/lockdown process as needed in combination with a blacklist strategy. The cloud side implements authentication and authorization, device registration and HTTP polling frequency, visitor/alarm records, member synchronization, and remote command closed-loop functions through Flask RESTful APIs, with MySQL handling data persistence. On the remote control side, MQTT serves as the primary communication channel, supplemented by HTTP polling as a fallback mechanism, thus ensuring reliable and timely message delivery and acknowledgment updates even during network fluctuations.
34: During actual construction and integration testing, the system successfully completed the closed loop of frame capture, detection, recognition, linkage, record keeping, and remote handling. The design philosophy for each link is as follows: the device side, under resource constraints, employs throttling and self-recovery mechanisms to ensure long-term reliable operation; the cloud side uses a command state machine to rigorously and orderly record the states of creation, delivery, execution, and result reporting, facilitating traceability and auditing; the mobile side uses a statistics dashboard and visitor list for daily information display, and employs a double-confirmation mechanism to reduce the probability of accidental triggering of high-risk operations. Thus, this system achieves a reproducible and trustworthy engineering closed loop on a low-cost platform, thereby naturally providing a deployable smart doorbell solution for home entrance scenarios.

56: Since the camera is capturing video frames continuously and doing real-time face detection and feature matching locally, it is natural and convenient to employ a configurable threshold strategy to discriminate between registered family members and unknown visitors, and for authorized users, it then activates multimodal feedback and an unlocking action (simulated by a stepper motor) with an appropriate duplication-avoidance mechanism.

83: As smart home and home security systems continue to evolve, the home entrance scenario has expanded from traditional video intercom to a composite application scenario integrating identity verification, event recording, and remote intervention. Express delivery, food delivery, property management, and temporary visitors are characterized by high frequency, short stays, and strong randomness. Without traceable event records and timely handling mechanisms, risks such as abnormal loitering and tailgating entry become difficult to identify promptly and audit afterwards [10][11].
84: Compared with indoor fixed scenarios, the doorstep scenario features short-term interaction, significant illumination variation, frequent occlusion and backlighting, and limited device computing power. Therefore, system design must simultaneously satisfy multiple requirements including second-level response, robust recognition, privacy protection, and long-term stable operation [9][12].
85: In recent years, the development of cloud-edge-device collaboration and edge intelligence has made it feasible to deploy lightweight vision models on low-cost embedded platforms such as Raspberry Pi. In the field of face recognition, the pipeline of detection, feature representation learning, and vector comparison has become relatively mature, with lightweight networks, model compression, and inference optimization becoming key technical routes for deployment on resource-constrained devices [6][8][13].
86: However, relying solely on edge-side offline processing is insufficient to meet the requirements of multi-terminal viewing, centralized storage, and remote handling. Therefore, smart doorbells oriented toward home security typically adopt a cloud-edge collaborative architecture: the edge side performs real-time perception and preliminary decision-making, the cloud side handles structured event management, command scheduling, and auditing, while the mobile side handles status display and high-risk operation interaction, thereby achieving a balance among real-time performance, availability, and traceability [12].
87: Based on the above background, this thesis designs and implements a smart doorbell and visitor management system with Raspberry Pi as the edge node, cloud services as the management center, and an Android client as the interaction entry point. The system provides identity verification and unlocking linkage for family members, snapshot capture and trace recording plus anomaly warning for unknown visitors, and enhances the manageability and controllability of home entrance scenarios through a remote control closed loop and security auditing mechanisms.
88: 1.2 Current Research Status at Home and Abroad
89: 1.2.1 Current Research Status of Smart Doorbell and Home Security Systems
90: Existing smart doorbell and home security systems generally feature video capture, event detection, and mobile-side notification as basic capabilities, gradually introducing advanced functions such as object recognition, abnormal behavior analysis, and cloud-based evidence storage [10]. Among these, cloud-centralized solutions facilitate unified model training, policy updates, and cross-device management, but are more sensitive to bandwidth, latency, and service availability, and are prone to problems such as delayed alerts and unstable control links under network jitter conditions.
91: From an architectural perspective, related research has mainly formed two technical routes: one is a centralized approach based on cloud intelligence, uploading recognition, analysis, and storage tasks to the cloud; the other is a distributed approach based on edge intelligence, completing real-time inference on the device side and only uploading structured events or evidence summaries to the cloud [9]. The latter has advantages in latency control, privacy protection, and weak-network availability, but imposes higher requirements on edge-side model lightweighting, resource scheduling, and system stability.
92: Moreover, the home entrance scenario involves multiple categories of subjects including family members, couriers, food delivery personnel, property staff, and temporary visitors. The system must not only improve recognition pass rates but also control false admission rates and false alarm rates. Therefore, research focus has expanded from single recognition accuracy to system-level capabilities including threshold strategy, anomaly handling, event tracking, audit trails, and operational observability.
93: 1.2.2 Current Research Status of Face Recognition and Edge Computing
94: Face recognition typically involves face detection, alignment, feature representation learning, and similarity discrimination. Currently, vector comparison based on deep feature embedding has become the mainstream technical paradigm [7]. In edge deployment scenarios, the research focus has shifted from solely pursuing accuracy to a comprehensive trade-off among accuracy, model size, inference latency, and energy consumption.
95: To adapt to resource-constrained devices, academia has conducted extensive research on lightweight network design, knowledge distillation, model compression, and inference optimization [14]. Meanwhile, factors such as cross-age variation, pose deflection, occlusion, and backlighting can significantly affect the stability of recognition features. Therefore, threshold calibration, sample quality control, consecutive frame stabilization, and anti-duplicate triggering mechanisms have become key supplementary strategies in engineering deployment [6].
96: In addition to recognition accuracy, edge-side face recognition systems also need to address issues such as incremental member database updates, feature persistence, anomaly self-recovery, and operational observability. Particularly in continuous video stream scenarios, systems typically need to maintain long-term stable operation through throttling control, caching mechanisms, and log monitoring, which is also an important evaluation dimension for whether edge intelligence can be practically deployed [9].
97: 1.2.3 Current Research Status of IoT Remote Control and Data Synchronization
98: Common implementation approaches for IoT remote control include polling, long-connection push, and publish/subscribe models. Compared with traditional HTTP polling, the MQTT-based publish/subscribe mechanism is more suitable for device control scenarios in terms of message payload, transmission latency, and scalability. Therefore, 'MQTT primary channel + HTTP polling fallback' has become a common engineering approach that balances low latency and high availability [12].
99: The core of remote control systems is not only message transmission but also command consistency, state observability, and execution traceability. To avoid command loss, duplicate execution, or state inconsistency, engineering practice typically introduces command state machines, result reporting, and audit recording mechanisms, constructing a closed-loop control chain from command creation, delivery, and execution to acknowledgment update [11][12].
100: In home security scenarios, remote unlocking and snapshot capture are high-risk operations, and the system must simultaneously satisfy low-latency response and strong security constraints. Therefore, related research generally emphasizes mechanisms such as identity authentication, device signing, nonce anti-replay, least-privilege control, and sensitive operation auditing to ensure the trustworthiness and accountability of the control chain.
102: This project takes the Raspberry Pi based smart doorbell system as the research object, and conducts system design around three core requirements in home entrance scenarios: identity verification, visitor trace recording, and remote handling. In consideration of the requirements for real-time performance, privacy, and weak-network availability in home security, this thesis adopts a system partitioning approach with collaboration among device side, cloud side, and mobile side.
103: Specifically, the device side is responsible for video capture, face detection and recognition, liveness verification, door lock linkage, and local caching; the cloud side is responsible for user authentication, device binding, member and visitor data management, command delivery, and result reporting; the mobile side is responsible for status display, history record query, and high-risk operation interaction. The cloud side provides unified service interfaces through RESTful APIs, combined with MySQL persistence and Redis caching for command and state management.
104: In terms of system objectives, this thesis focuses on four categories of engineering metrics: first, edge-side real-time performance, i.e., the recognition pipeline can match the short-stay interaction at the doorstep; second, recognition reliability, i.e., reducing false recognition and missed recognition through threshold strategy, sample management, and consecutive frame stabilization; third, control reachability, i.e., maintaining the closed loop of command delivery and result reporting under network fluctuation conditions; fourth, security auditability, i.e., performing structured recording of liveness detection failures, high-risk controls, and abnormal events, satisfying the 'low false admission priority' access control constraint [1][4].
106: The main characteristics of this work are reflected in three aspects: first, adopting a cloud-edge-device collaborative architecture combining edge-side local recognition with cloud-side centralized management, reducing the risk of raw sensitive data transmission while ensuring real-time response capability [9]; second, designing an MQTT push + heartbeat polling fallback hybrid delivery mechanism for the remote control link, to improve command reachability and system availability in weak-network environments; third, introducing a command closed loop and audit log mechanism, enabling remote commands to have full-process state tracking capability covering creation, delivery, execution, and traceability.
107: From an engineering application perspective, this thesis implements an integrated closed loop of identity recognition, liveness verification, door lock linkage, visitor management, and remote control on a low-cost embedded platform, with targeted optimization for real deployment issues such as resource constraints, network fluctuations, and security auditing. This design not only satisfies the graduation design requirements for a complete system implementation but also possesses the engineering foundation for evolution toward home access control and smart doorbell prototype systems.
109: The overall structure of this thesis is arranged as follows: Chapter 1 is the introduction; Chapter 2 analyzes system feasibility, functional requirements, and non-functional requirements; Chapter 3 presents the overall design and business processes; Chapter 4 introduces the software design of cloud services and the Android client; Chapter 5 elaborates on the hardware solution and device-side software design; Chapter 6 describes system implementation and results analysis; Chapter 7 summarizes the entire thesis and discusses future work.
113: From a technical implementation perspective, Raspberry Pi already possesses the basic capability to run lightweight vision models and IoT communication components, supporting tasks such as video capture, face detection, feature comparison, and remote control. To address the limitations of edge device computing power and memory, the system controls resource consumption through mechanisms such as frame skipping, recognition throttling, and anomaly self-recovery, and performs engineering trade-offs among resolution, processing frequency, and recognition latency.
115: Face data constitutes sensitive personal information, and system design must follow principles of minimum necessity, purpose limitation, explicit notification, and security protection. This thesis moves recognition and liveness verification as far forward as possible to the edge side, uploading only structured event records and necessary snapshot evidence to the cloud, thereby reducing the privacy exposure risk brought by centralized storage and large-scale transmission of raw face data [12].
117: The system hardware consists of general-purpose components such as Raspberry Pi, camera, buzzer, and stepper motor/driver board, with relatively low overall cost and manageable procurement and maintenance difficulty. The software side uses Python, Flask, MySQL, Redis, MQTT, and Android ecosystem components, with moderate development threshold and high reusability, suitable for graduation design verification and prototype system iteration [14].
119: With the continuous growth of home security and smart home demands, smart doorbells with identity verification, event recording, and remote handling capabilities have clear application value. In particular, edge-side local recognition and cloud-edge collaboration mechanisms simultaneously address privacy protection, low-latency response, and weak-network availability, aligning with the current trend of smart home systems evolving toward security, real-time performance, and trustworthiness [12].
122: As an edge execution unit, the device side needs to simultaneously possess perception, decision-making, execution, and trace-recording capabilities. Specifically, the system should provide stable video capture, face detection and recognition, liveness detection, buzzer alerts, door lock linkage, unknown visitor snapshot capture, local caching, and anomaly self-recovery, and support configurable parameters such as resolution, frame capture frequency, recognition throttling, and cooldown window, to adapt to the short-stay and environmental fluctuation characteristics of the doorstep scenario [1][5].
124: The cloud side needs to abstract user operations into deliverable, trackable, and auditable control commands. After a command is created, it should be persistently stored and delivered to the device through the MQTT primary channel or heartbeat polling fallback; after the device executes it, the status and result fields are written back, thus forming a complete command closed loop and audit chain.
125: In addition to remote control, the cloud side also undertakes responsibilities including user authentication, family and device binding, online status maintenance, visitor/alarm record persistence, and mobile-side query support. The core requirement is to ensure consistency, traceability, and controllable unauthorized access risk for multi-terminal access through permission boundaries, state synchronization, and structured data management.
127: The Android side is the primary interaction entry point for users and needs to simultaneously satisfy information display efficiency and high-risk operation constraints. Its basic capabilities include login/registration and session maintenance, homepage statistics dashboard, device status viewing, visitor record review, member management, and photo uploading. For high-risk operations such as remote unlocking, it should also provide explicit interaction confirmation and result feedback mechanisms.
130: Performance requirements are mainly reflected in three aspects: first, the edge side should maintain a stable frame rate at common resolutions and control the response latency from recognition to linkage execution within seconds; second, the recognition pipeline should reduce false recognition rates through threshold calibration, consecutive frame stabilization, and sample quality control; third, the remote control link should achieve low-latency delivery when network conditions permit, and maintain command reachability through the polling mechanism when the primary channel is abnormal [9].
132: Access control admission is a typical high-risk authorization scenario. In addition to user-side authentication and device-side trusted communication, the system must also possess detection capabilities against presentation attacks such as photo attacks, video replay, and screen recapture [4][15]. Therefore, this thesis introduces liveness detection as a secondary verification after member recognition, combined with multi-frame capture, local motion cues, and cloud-side conservative review mechanisms to reduce the false admission probability, following the fail-close and low false admission priority security strategy [2][3].
133: Security requirements further include: first, mobile-side access requires Token verification and permission control; second, device communication needs to combine signature and nonce mechanisms to suppress forgery and replay risks; third, structured auditing of high-risk events such as remote unlocking, liveness detection failure, and anomalous access should be performed to support post-incident tracing and responsibility delineation.
135: Reliability requirements include three aspects: first, business continuity under network fluctuation conditions, i.e., supporting local caching, offline-to-online resumption, and push-plus-polling dual-channel fallback; second, device-side long-term operational reliability, i.e., reducing the probability of freezing and non-responsiveness through single-instance constraints, resource contention isolation, and frame capture failure self-recovery mechanisms; third, full-link exception handling capability, i.e., both the cloud side and device side need to provide clear error states, retry strategies, and log output.
137: Maintainability and extensibility are mainly reflected in: first, the device side, cloud side, and Android side adopt layered and modular design, facilitating subsequent functional iteration and problem localization; second, key configurations such as recognition threshold, polling interval, MQTT connection parameters, and liveness detection strategy should support parameterized management; third, system interfaces and data structures should reserve boundaries for subsequent expansion to multi-device access and more security policies.
140: This system adopts a three-tier collaborative overall architecture comprising device-side local recognition, cloud-side centralized management, and mobile-side remote control. The device side is responsible for video capture, face detection and recognition, visitor recording, and local linkage.
144: In terms of data flow design, the structured events collected by the device side, such as visitor type, time, similarity, and snapshot image path, are first uploaded to the cloud via API. While persisting the data, the cloud simultaneously exposes two types of interfaces—paginated query and statistical analysis—for mobile-side use. Remote control is initiated by the mobile side; the cloud generates commands and reliably and timely delivers them to the device side for execution via the MQTT/heartbeat channel, and finally the device side reports the execution results to the cloud. This design fully embodies the philosophy of edge computing and cloud management.
146: 3.2.1 Face Recognition and Event Processing Flow
147: To illustrate the system's processing logic in member recognition, unknown visitor handling, liveness verification, and data synchronization, this thesis presents the face recognition and event processing flowchart shown in Fig 3.2.
149: Fig 3.2 Face Recognition and Event Processing Flowchart
150: The system first captures video frames and detects face regions, then extracts features and performs identity determination. If recognized as a family member, it enters the local anti-photo detection and AI liveness review process; upon passing liveness verification, it executes unlocking and records the family visit event; if not passed, it blocks unlocking and records the liveness failure event. If the recognition result is not in the member database, it is determined as an unknown visitor, and snapshot capture, visitor event recording, and monitoring are triggered. All types of events are ultimately uploaded to the cloud or locally cached depending on network status, thus forming a complete closed loop of recognition, handling, and synchronization.
151: 3.2.2 Unknown Visitor Snapshot and Alert Flow
152: When the recognition result cannot match any entry in the member database, the system determines it as an unknown visitor and performs snapshot capture, generating a visitor record containing time, snapshot image, and recognition confidence information. If abnormal loitering by the unknown visitor is detected or blacklist rules are triggered, the alert process is activated, i.e., the buzzer alarms, the system locks down, and alerts and evidence are uploaded for traceability.
153: 3.2.3 Visitor Record Upload and Cloud Notification Flow
154: After the device side uploads visitor records through the cloud interface, the cloud performs persistent storage and naturally and timely updates statistical data. Abnormal events are recorded in alarm logs by the cloud, and data is actively and reliably provided to the mobile side through caching/messaging mechanisms. During network fluctuations, the device side first records data in local cache and performs batch resumption after network recovery, thus well ensuring data integrity.
156: After the mobile side initiates a remote unlock, alarm, voice, or snapshot request, the cloud creates a command and writes it to the command queue, with the initial command state being pending. During the delivery phase, priority is given to pushing the command to the device-side subscription topic via MQTT.
158: Fig 3.3 Remote Command Closed-Loop Sequence Diagram
160: To illustrate the transmission relationship of remote control requests among the mobile side, cloud side, and device side, this thesis takes remote unlocking as an example and sorts out the processing process from command initiation, verification, and delivery to execution and reporting, as shown in Fig 3.4.
164: After the user initiates a remote unlock request on the APP side, the cloud first completes identity verification, permission verification, and device online status judgment. If the verification fails or the device is offline, the request is directly rejected with a prompt message returned. If conditions are met, the cloud generates an unlock command and delivers it to the device side. After obtaining the command, the device executes the unlock operation and reports the execution result back to the cloud. Finally, the APP displays the processing result and generates an operation record, thus forming a complete remote control command closed loop.
166: Member information is saved to the cloud after being entered through the mobile side or management side. The device side periodically synchronizes the member list and face data, and updates the local feature database.

172: Device-side modules mainly include: camera capture module, face recognition module, visitor management and local persistence module, interaction and alert module, data synchronization module, remote control execution module, and security protection module. Among these, face recognition and linkage handling are completed locally; data synchronization and remote control are responsible for interacting with the cloud, reducing module coupling.
174: Cloud-side modules mainly include: authentication module, family and member management module, device management and heartbeat module, visitor and alarm module, remote command module, blacklist module, and file service module. 178: The system follows the security principles of user-side authentication, device-side trusted communication, and data minimization in its overall design. Users must carry a JWT Token when accessing protected cloud resources, with the binding relationship among users, families, and devices serving as the permission boundary. Device-side requests adopt signature verification combined with a nonce mechanism to prevent replay attacks. At the same time, the system prioritizes completing face recognition and liveness verification at the edge side, uploading only necessary structured event data and snapshot evidence to the cloud, and performing desensitization processing on sensitive information, thereby simultaneously addressing privacy protection, communication security, and audit traceability.
181: This chapter elaborates on the software implementation design from two parts—cloud services and the Android client—focusing on data models, interface boundaries, communication links, and security mechanisms, and presents key module implementation points.
182: 4.2 Detailed Design of Cloud Service System
183: 4.2.1 Overall Cloud Architecture and Directory Organization
184: The most problematic issue during integration testing is the inconsistency among mobile-side interface fields, cloud return structures, and device-side reporting fields. Therefore, this project has made appropriate designs on the cloud side, namely: a unified return encapsulation format, clearly defined error code conventions, retention of necessary request information in logs, and desensitization processing of sensitive fields, making problems traceable, reproducible, and easier to fix.
185: In actual implementation, the cloud side uses Flask to build RESTful APIs, dividing routes by functions such as authentication, devices, visitors/alarms, members/blacklists, and remote control. Correspondingly, MySQL is used to persist core business data including visitors, alarms, commands, and device status; Redis is used for nonce verification and a small amount of caching; MQTT is specifically responsible for low-latency command push; resources such as snapshots and member photos are stored in file directories, with each interface returning their accessible paths for mobile-side calls.
186: The positioning of the cloud side is very clear: to 'collect, store, and retrieve' the data reported by the device side, while translating mobile-side operations into commands, delivering them to devices, and finally obtaining and recording acknowledgments. Therefore, the cloud side is not simply a pile of interfaces, but is implemented around data management, command closed loops, and permission boundaries.

217: Statistical interfaces are essentially designed for daily aggregation and categorized counting, requiring the separation of family member and stranger counts by visitor_type, as well as TOP statistics for alarm causes. Engineering-wise, it is reasonable to avoid placing all statistical computation on the client side: the mobile side only displays aggregated results, thus reducing client burden while maintaining consistency of data dimensions.
218: Since visitor records and alarm records are the most frequently accessed data on the mobile side, lists need pagination processing, details should be traceable, and the homepage should have statistics. Moreover, since the most commonly used filter conditions for user queries are device_id, created_at (time window), and handled (processing status), indexes need to be established on these fields to support pagination and time-range queries.
221: The authentication module includes interfaces for user registration, login, Token refresh, and user information query. After the mobile side successfully logs in, it obtains a JWT Token, and subsequent access to protected resources must carry the Authorization header in HTTP request headers. Therefore, interface design should naturally consider issues such as unified error codes and prompts, secure password handling, Token lifecycle management, and permission boundary constraints.
223: This design transforms push instability from an uncontrollable risk into an explainable and controllable state. When MQTT is disconnected, the device will pull pending commands for continued execution during the next heartbeat, which leads to another consideration: the polling interval is not simply 'the smaller the better'—too short an interval actually increases server burden and device-side network overhead. Therefore, the combination of 'MQTT primary channel + HTTP polling' was ultimately adopted, with parameters reasonably adjusted according to the actual network environment during deployment, prioritizing overall stability.
224: The fundamental issue of device management interfaces is not whether they can be accessed, but whether they can run stably over the long term. Therefore, after the device side starts up, it must first complete registration and identity authentication, then report heartbeats at fixed intervals to declare online status. Consequently, the heartbeat interface designed in this project serves an engineering purpose: when the MQTT push link is abnormal, it can return a list of pending commands as a fallback channel.
226: The visitor module includes interfaces for visitor upload, list pagination, detail query, and statistics. After the device side recognizes a visitor, it uploads the visitor record to the cloud for storage, and then provides it to the mobile side for review. In all cases where visitor_type is stranger or abnormal logic is triggered, the cloud will timely and reliably write to alarm_logs to record the alarm event. Therefore, the alarm module naturally provides alarm list and handling interfaces, allowing users to confirm, annotate, and mark abnormal events as handled, thus naturally forming a complete and manageable security event chain.
228: The member module provides interfaces for member list, addition, deletion, and update, and supports member photo uploading for device-side feature database construction and update. The blacklist module provides blacklist entry management, device-side synchronization interfaces, and match reporting interfaces.
229: (5) Remote Control Interfaces and Command Closed Loop
230: In interface design, the cloud side imposes enumeration constraints on command types and performs stricter permission verification for high-risk operations, which naturally helps restrict users to only operate their bound devices.
231: After the device side completes execution, it timely and reliably reports the result (success/failure, error reason, relevant evidence path, etc.) back to the cloud, so the cloud can promptly update the command status and timestamp fields. Therefore, the system can clearly distinguish situations such as command not delivered, command delivered but not executed, and execution failed, which also facilitates forming standardized audit records.
232: Remote control is the most perceptible and highest-risk function for users, so this project has designed remote control in a layered manner: the uncontrollable factor of 'one-click direct execution' is completely avoided by having the mobile side initiate the request first, then the cloud creates a command record and persists it, and only then does the command get transmitted to the device side for execution through the communication channel.
233: In addition to remote control, the cloud side adds a liveness detection interface POST /api/liveness/check for device-side invocation. The interface receives device_id, member_name, and multi-frame images, and returns fields such as live/score/reason/provider.
235: (1) User-Side JWT Verification and Permission Boundary
236: The user side uses JWT to implement stateless authentication. The cloud side performs validity verification on Tokens carried in all protected interfaces, reasonably uses the binding relationships among users, families, and devices to restrict resource access scope, and for high-risk interfaces such as remote unlocking, should additionally add device ownership verification.
238: Device-side communication introduces signature authentication. The cloud side can verify the legitimacy of requests based on device identification and shared keys, while device requests carry random numbers (nonce). The cloud writes nonce values into Redis with appropriate expiration times; any duplicate nonce found is treated as a replay attack and directly rejected. Thus, device communication security can be greatly improved without adopting a complex certificate system.
241: During deployment and integration testing, this project is more concerned with whether the connection is stable, whether messages may be lost, and whether status can be reported back. Therefore, rather than targeting a specific fixed latency value, the approach is to use the heartbeat fallback channel to ensure reachability when the push link fluctuates, thereby converging system risk.
242: The MQTT push channel facilitates fast command delivery. Therefore, the cloud publishes commands to topics divided by device dimension, and the device side maintains a persistent subscription to that topic to receive commands. The advantages of this approach in a home network environment are low bandwidth consumption and friendly interaction latency, but it must be acknowledged that engineering details such as reconnection, subscription recovery, and abnormal disconnection must also be handled.
244: During project debugging, after enabling MQTT as the primary channel, command delivery latency was significantly improved compared to pure polling. At the same time, retaining the heartbeat interface to pull pending commands as a fallback allows delivery and status updates to continue even during brief network instability.
245: (3) Command State Transition and Result Reporting
246: Integration testing experience shows that the vast majority of problems are not unimplemented functions, but rather a step in the chain being stuck. Specifically, a command staying at pending indicates it has not yet been delivered; entering delivered but not executed is generally due to device-side execution failure or acknowledgment reporting failure. Therefore, using status fields and timestamps makes problem localization more direct and convenient, and also facilitates providing clear prompts on the mobile side.
247: The command state machine transforms remote control from a one-time request into a traceable process. Therefore, the cloud maintains a status field for each command, simultaneously recording important time points such as created_at, delivered_at, and executed_at. After the device side reports the result and failure reason, the cloud updates the status and saves the result.
249: The system contains resource files such as member photos and visitor snapshots. Therefore, the cloud uses upload interfaces to upload files to designated directories, and then provides corresponding resource URLs to the mobile side. For this purpose, during engineering deployment, upload types and file sizes should be reasonably restricted, path formats standardized, and security vulnerabilities such as directory traversal eliminated. Finally, combined with access control policies, resources are only made accessible to authorized users.
251: 4.3 Detailed Design of Android Client System
253: Rapid iteration is needed during the graduation design phase, so the structure used should be more conducive to interface changes: when interfaces change, only modifications at the ApiService/Repository layer are needed, with very few page-side changes, making integration debugging and troubleshooting very convenient.
254: In implementation, a layered organization approach is adopted to reduce coupling: the UI layer handles interface display and interaction processing; the Repository serves as the business entry point to uniformly encapsulate interface calls and data transformation; the network layer uses Retrofit+OkHttp to handle requests and interceptor logic; local storage is used to save Tokens and necessary user information.
255: The goal of the mobile side is very direct: to allow users to see what is happening at the doorstep while having remote handling capabilities. Therefore, the client pages are designed with three high-frequency tasks as the core: visitor record review, member management, and remote control.
256: 4.3.2 Network Layer and Data Layer Design
258: During integration testing, the most common problems are authentication failure and field inconsistency: for example, Token expiration causing 401, or server-side field name adjustments causing parsing failure. Therefore, in addition to basic logging, the network layer needs to transparently transmit error codes and error messages to the upper layer, combined with Toast/dialog prompts to notify users, and guide re-login when necessary. This kind of 'explainable error' experience often enhances user trust in the system more than merely pursuing request success rates.
259: The client network layer centrally defines cloud interfaces in ApiService, avoiding scattered code for assembling URLs and request headers across various pages. Retrofit is responsible for converting interface definitions into callable methods, while OkHttp uniformly handles Token appending, log output, and timeout strategy through interceptors.
261: The client uses data model classes to carry various structures returned by the cloud, such as login responses, visitor records, and statistical information, using Gson for field mapping. The client also performs corresponding error handling for various situations such as network exceptions, server exceptions, and authentication failures: user-perceptible errors are prompted through Toast or dialog boxes with appropriate guidance for re-login, while errors during development and debugging are combined with log output and interface return information, greatly facilitating problem localization.
263: The Repository layer encapsulates businesses such as authentication, visitors, members, and remote control, shielding underlying interface details. For example, after successful login, the Repository is responsible for saving the Token and maintaining the session; the visitor list interface has pagination parameters and data transformation handled by the Repository; the remote control interface is uniformly encapsulated by the Repository for command types and request payloads, reducing maintenance costs caused by scattered UI layer business logic.
264: The Repository layer provides good encapsulation for various businesses such as authentication, visitors, members, and remote control, thus shielding underlying interface details: after successful login, the Repository saves the Token and manages the session; the visitor list interface is handled by the Repository for pagination parameters and data transformation; the remote control interface is uniformly encapsulated by the Repository for command types and request payloads, thereby reducing maintenance costs caused by scattered UI layer business logic.
267: The client has two interfaces for login and registration. When users enter their account credentials, authentication is performed; successful login enters the main interface, while authentication failure displays an error prompt and allows users to retry. The purpose of registration is to create a new user and complete basic information initialization, naturally leading to subsequent family and device binding.
268: From Fig 4.1 and Fig 4.2, the login and registration interfaces can be clearly and naturally seen. The client first checks input completeness before submitting the authentication request. After successful login, it enters the main interface, while the registration process is used to create a new user and initialize basic profile information, also preparing for subsequent family and device binding.

When the application starts, it first reads the local Token: if it exists and is valid, it enters the main interface; otherwise, it jumps to the login page. Therefore, the page displays various indicators aggregated by the cloud: today's visitor count, 7-day trend, counts of family members/strangers, whether there are unhandled alarms, etc. Placing statistical computation on the cloud has very clear benefits: first, the mobile side does not need to pull large amounts of historical records in weak-network environments; second, all statistical dimensions are unified, so the statistical indicators referenced in the subsequent testing chapter of the thesis are naturally consistent and directly usable.
286: From the link perspective: the client does not directly control the device, but rather calls the cloud interface to create a command, which the cloud reliably delivers to the device side for execution, and then displays the result based on the updated acknowledgment. Therefore, this design reasonably and centrally places risk and traceability on the cloud side. Users only need to see command created/delivered/executed/failure reason, without needing to care about underlying MQTT and heartbeat details.
287: The remote control entry primarily includes operations such as unlock, alarm, and snapshot. From the interaction perspective, it is clearly evident that remote unlocking is a high-risk operation—once mistakenly operated, it can cause irreversible consequences. Therefore, the client imposes two layers of thorough and reasonable constraints on the unlock operation: first, a second confirmation, and second, a clear status prompt after command execution, preventing users from repeatedly sending commands during network fluctuations.

318: 4.3.9 Interaction Experience Optimization and Engineering Practice
319: In home security applications, interaction experience not only affects usability but also influences users' subjective perception of system reliability and trustworthiness. Therefore, the client emphasizes state visibility in page design: providing clear feedback for loading, empty data, and error scenarios, avoiding users mistakenly believing the system has failed. For example, the visitor list displays a loading state during first entry and pull-to-refresh; when there are no records, it shows an empty state prompt; when there are network exceptions or interface errors, it provides a retry entry and explanation of the cause.
320: In terms of engineering practice, the client reduces business fragmentation through unified network encapsulation and Repository entry: authentication-related logic is concentrated in the session management module, avoiding Token handling scattered across pages; image loading uses Glide caching strategy to reduce repeated requests, improving browsing experience in weak-network scenarios.
321: 4.3.10 Permission Boundaries and High-Risk Operation Interaction Design
322: Since remote unlocking is a high-risk operation, the mobile-side design must necessarily balance convenience and security. Therefore, the client uses the login Token as the basic credential and the family/device binding relationship as the resource access boundary, effectively restricting access to visitor records, member information, and remote control interfaces to only bound users.
323: Moreover, to avoid the experience issue where something appears to be clicked but does not actually take effect, the client should actively refresh device status or pull command execution results after completing key operations, mapping the cloud-managed command closed-loop state to the UI (i.e., pending, delivered, executed, execution failed). Upon execution failure, the client should prompt the user to check device online status, network connection, and permission settings, and provide a retry entry.
325: During actual mobile-side deployment, different Android system versions, different manufacturer ROMs, and different permission policies must inevitably be faced. Therefore, the client must thoroughly adapt storage permissions, network permissions, and background operation restrictions, while setting reasonable timeout parameters for image loading and network requests. Consequently, this project entrusts sensitive information such as Tokens to an encrypted storage component, while API Base URL, timeout parameters, and log switches are all handled as configuration items, facilitating debugging and release switching.
326: In terms of functional expansion, existing modules reserve structural space for subsequent capability enhancement: on one hand, push notifications (e.g., real-time alarm event push) can be introduced to improve timeliness; on the other hand, real-time video preview can be expanded, combined with more comprehensive local caching and pagination strategies to improve weak-network experience. When the system scale expands, ViewModel and observable state management can be further introduced to decouple page states from the UI layer, improving maintainability in complex interaction scenarios.
330: The system hardware uses Raspberry Pi as the core control and edge computing platform, with a camera for capturing doorstep video streams, and a buzzer and stepper motor for alert prompts and unlocking linkage. Therefore, the hardware solution adheres to the principles of low cost, reproducibility, and easy deployment: all selected components and interfaces are general-purpose (CSI, USB, GPIO), making it very suitable for graduation design prototype verification and on-site demonstration.
331: Functionally, the hardware system can be hierarchically divided into computing and control module, image capture module, interaction and alert module, actuator module, and power supply and connectivity module. It is worth noting that the computing and capture modules determine recognition performance and real-time capability, while the actuator module determines the effectiveness and stability of unlocking linkage. The relationships among the parts are shown in Fig 5.1.
335: From Fig 4.1, it can be seen that the device-side data flow and control flow can be reasonably divided into four clear stages: capture, recognition, linkage, and synchronization. Specifically, the camera outputs video frames through the CSI/USB interface, and the Raspberry Pi captures frames in the main loop, performs preprocessing and frame-skipping throttling, then invokes the dlib solution for face detection and feature extraction, and subsequently performs distance comparison against the local member feature database to obtain recognition results. If a family member is recognized and the system is not currently locked down, the control module drives the buzzer alarm through GPIO and triggers door lock linkage.
336: To verify the reproducibility of the discussed solution and the peripheral linkage effects, this thesis physically assembled various peripherals such as the camera, buzzer, and stepper motor/driver board on the Raspberry Pi platform, as shown in detail in Fig 5.2.
340: 5.2 Raspberry Pi and Camera Module Selection
342: Since Raspberry Pi has an excellent hardware and software ecosystem and ample GPIO resources, it is an ideal choice for edge-side deployment in doorstep scenarios. Therefore, in this project, Raspberry Pi is used to run the main face recognition program, control peripherals, and simultaneously perform data synchronization with the cloud. Compared with more expensive industrial computers or specialized edge computing boxes, Raspberry Pi can well satisfy real-time processing requirements while greatly reducing hardware costs, and is more conducive to using scripts and systemd services to achieve automatic startup and automatic operation.
344: As the image capture module, the camera's clarity and stability directly affect recognition performance. Therefore, this system preferentially selects the Raspberry Pi CSI interface camera to establish a stable capture link, while reasonably configuring the capture resolution to 640×480 at the software layer, with the frame rate strategy also optimized accordingly. When deployment environment restrictions prevent the use of a CSI camera, USB cameras are extended as alternative input sources. More importantly, considering the real-time requirements of the doorstep scenario and the constraints of edge-side computing power, the system preferentially uses medium resolution to increase frame rate and speed up response while ensuring recognizability.
347: The buzzer is used to provide multimodal feedback, including recognition success tones, unknown visitor alert tones, and abnormal scenario alarm tones. The buzzer is controlled through GPIO for switching or PWM control, and can implement modes such as short beep, dual-tone beep, and long alarm beep, enhancing user perception of system status. In doorstep scenarios, alert tones are not only used for interaction feedback but can also serve as a lightweight security deterrent.
350: 5.3.2 Stepper Motor Unlocking Simulation and Drive Design
351: This project uses a 28BYJ-48 reduction stepper motor with a ULN2003 driver board to simulate door lock opening and closing actions. Compared to simple on/off control with relays, the stepper motor can more intuitively demonstrate the 'unlock/lock' action process, facilitating graduation design demonstration.

356: 5.4 Software Architecture and Main Loop Design
357: The device side is critical to the system's real-time performance and availability. Therefore, this project adopts a modular design, decoupling various functions such as video capture, face recognition, visitor management, interaction and alert, data synchronization, remote control execution, and security protection into independent modules, which are then unified and orchestrated by the main program. The main loop uses the basic closed loop of frame capture, recognition-handling-reporting-command reception-execution and acknowledgment to appropriately handle two types of scenarios: local admission and abnormal alerts.
358: Since the device side reasonably separates periodic tasks such as heartbeat reporting and command pulling from real-time tasks such as frame capture and recognition in its concurrency design, the real-time link runs at a higher frequency in the main loop, while periodic links use independent threads or timing mechanisms to reduce blocking impact on the main loop. More importantly, to prevent multi-process competition for camera and GPIO resources from causing stuttering or erroneous actions, the system explicitly adopts a single-instance operation mode and is equipped with comprehensive resource release and reconstruction mechanisms.
360: 5.5.1 Frame Capture Strategy and Resolution Configuration
361: The camera module is responsible for obtaining real-time frames from the CSI/USB camera. To achieve a stable frame rate under edge-side computing constraints, this project sets the common resolution to 640×480 and adopts a latest-frame-first processing strategy: when the recognition pipeline processing speed is lower than the camera output speed, the latest frame is processed first to reduce end-to-end latency. This strategy better meets user experience requirements in doorstep short-interaction scenarios.
362: 5.5.2 Frame Capture Failure Detection and Self-Recovery Mechanism
363: In actual deployment, camera frame capture may encounter various situations such as resource occupation, driver anomalies, and temporary jitter. Therefore, directly ignoring frame capture failures would cause the system to freeze at the welcome interface or have no display for extended periods. Consequently, the main loop counts consecutive frame capture failures, and when the count reaches a set threshold, it automatically triggers the self-recovery process of releasing capture resources and reinitializing the camera, thus naturally and reasonably reducing the frequency of manual intervention and effectively improving the system's long-term operational reliability.
364: 5.5.3 Latest Frame Supply and Snapshot Reuse
365: Since this project needs to implement remote snapshot capture and evidence collection, the concept of a frame provider is naturally and reasonably introduced in the remote control execution module: during snapshot capture, the camera is not reinitialized; instead, the image is directly taken from the latest frame cache maintained in the main loop, encoded as JPG, and uploaded. This also naturally avoids additional visual dependencies and the need for camera resource re-entry, thus effectively improving both the snapshot success rate and result consistency.
367: To balance real-time performance, stability, and false recognition risk in doorstep scenarios, this system introduces several key parameters and engineering strategies into the recognition pipeline, as shown in Table 5.1.
368: Table 5.1 Face Recognition Key Parameters and Engineering Strategies
369: Among these, frame skipping and minimum recognition interval jointly limit the recognition invocation frequency, prioritizing resource controllability under 24×7 operation; the distance threshold is used to balance the admission rate and false recognition risk; the action cooldown window and frame capture self-recovery strategy respectively address hardware linkage safety and device availability, enabling recognition results to be stably deployed in a manner closer to engineering products.
371: 5.6.1 Feature Database Construction and Member Registration
372: The member feature database is the foundation of face recognition. The system maintains a name identifier and corresponding face feature vector for each family member, and supports sample collection through the camera for registration. In actual use, sample quality factors such as clarity, pose, and illumination significantly affect recognition stability. Therefore, the member registration phase should cover multi-angle and multi-illumination samples as much as possible, and remove abnormal samples to reduce subsequent false recognition risk. The feature database construction and update flow is shown in Fig 5.6.
374: Fig 5.5 Face Database Construction and Management Flowchart
375: In terms of face database management, upon startup, the device side preferentially loads the cache file faces_cache.pkl to avoid traversing the sample directory and recalculating feature vectors each time it starts. When the cache does not exist, is corrupted, or member samples have been updated, the system falls back to traversing data/faces/<member> and rebuilding the feature database to generate a new cache. This mechanism can significantly shorten cold start time and maintain recognition capability in offline scenarios.
379: During the recognition phase, features are first extracted from the detected face and similarity comparison is performed against the member database. Then, based on the selected threshold, admission is determined: if the similarity is above the threshold, the face is judged as a member; otherwise, it is judged as an unknown visitor. Since images captured at different camera positions and under different lighting conditions have different characteristics, the threshold should be reasonably configured. In access control scenarios with extremely high security requirements, the threshold should be set to minimize the false recognition rate as much as possible, while correspondingly allowing necessary rejections to be assisted and confirmed through the mobile side.
380: 5.6.3 Consecutive Frame Stabilization and Anti-Duplicate Triggering
381: Since consecutive frames in the video stream contain jitter and noise, the system performs stabilization processing on recognition results and adds a cooldown window for action execution, preventing the same member from being recognized multiple times within a short period, which would cause repeated unlocking. This mechanism is particularly important in hardware linkage scenarios, as it can reduce mechanical wear and safety hazards caused by frequent motor and lock body movements, while improving user experience.
382: 5.6.4 Liveness Detection and Photo Attack Protection
383: Photo attacks/screen recapture in doorstep scenarios are a real risk: an attacker may hold a printed photo or mobile phone screen close to the camera. If the system only relies on single-frame feature comparison, there is a possibility of false admission. To reduce this risk, this project adds liveness verification as a secondary confirmation step between recognition as a known member and unlocking execution; only after liveness is verified is door lock linkage permitted.
384: Liveness detection adopts a combined strategy of heuristic + AI review. The device side consecutively captures multiple frames within the same recognition session based on face_box, and calculates frame differences for observability.
385: In engineering implementation, the system supports a two-vote mechanism to reduce false rejection caused by occasional failure to capture motion from live persons: a maximum of two reviews are performed within the same recognition session, and passing any one of them at the threshold allows admission; if not passed, unlocking is blocked with a buzzer alert, while events are still recorded according to the visitor/access log process, facilitating subsequent troubleshooting and parameter tuning.

389: The system abstracts each valid visit into a visitor record. The structured data with fields such as timestamp, visitor type, member name, similarity or confidence information, snapshot image path, and alarm identifier is not only conducive to local review and statistics, but also suitable for uploading to the cloud to form historical records viewable from any device.
390: 5.7.2 Local Database and Offline Caching Mechanism
391: The device side must continue to work normally during network fluctuations and when the cloud is unreachable. Therefore, visitor records and related alarm evidence should first be saved locally. The system uses a local database/file approach to store records and images, while recording the upload status of each entry. After network recovery, they are uploaded in batch in queue order, thus achieving offline-to-online resumption with no data loss. For home doorstep scenarios, this is an extremely reliable critical event traceability mechanism.
393: The system adopts multimodal feedback to enhance perceptibility: buzzer alerts upon successful recognition, alarm tones triggered in abnormal scenarios; in optional touchscreen scenarios, recognition results and status information can also be displayed. For scenarios such as unknown visitor loitering, the system can trigger early warnings based on threshold and time strategies, and record alarm logs for subsequent statistics and analysis.
394: 5.9 Data Synchronization and Remote Control Execution
396: The device side uses the cloud communication module to complete functions such as login, device registration, heartbeat reporting, visitor record upload, and member synchronization. It also adopts the approach of device requests carrying signature information combined with the cloud-side nonce verification mechanism, thus well implementing basic device-side authentication capability. Moreover, device communication fully considers availability and diagnosability, with key requests and error reasons being reliably logged.
397: 5.9.2 MQTT Command Channel and Heartbeat Fallback
398: Since remote control must necessarily balance low latency and high availability, the system adopts MQTT topic subscription for receiving commands as the primary channel, enabling fast and reliable command delivery under normal network conditions, supplemented by HTTP polling as a fallback channel to prevent commands from completely failing when MQTT is unavailable. During deployment and integration testing, careful optimization was performed on heartbeat parameters and MQTT connection strategy, greatly reducing the arrival and execution latency of operations such as remote unlocking and snapshot capture, very well suiting the timely handling requirements of home doorstep scenarios.
400: After receiving a command, the device side's remote control module directly executes actions such as unlocking and snapshot capture, and reports the execution result back to the cloud to update the command status. This closed-loop mechanism is very suitable for displaying execution status on the mobile side, and also facilitates troubleshooting issues such as command delay, device offline, and hardware failure.
402: The device side has clear and comprehensive configuration items for setting parameters such as recognition threshold, frame rate/resolution, heartbeat interval, MQTT connection parameters, and data directories. By adopting a configuration-based design, the system can flexibly adapt to different home environments and network conditions without modifying code. Moreover, the system performs status log recording for each critical path including frame capture, recognition, upload, and command execution, along with single-instance constraints and self-recovery mechanisms, achieving excellent maintainability.
403: 5.11 Device-Side State Machine and Concurrency Model Design
404: During operation, the device side needs to coordinate the real-time recognition link and the periodic communication link. To reduce coupling and improve stability, the system can be abstracted into several states: initialization—initializing the camera, GPIO, member database, and network components; running—continuously capturing frames, recognizing, and handling; degraded—entering offline caching mode when the network is unavailable; alarm—triggering alerts when blacklist matches or abnormal loitering is detected; recovery—rebuilding resources after frame capture failure, etc.
405: In terms of the concurrency model, the main thread maintains the real-time performance of recognition and linkage actions; periodic tasks such as member synchronization and command pulling are placed in background threads or scheduled task execution. When MQTT is introduced, command reception can be triggered by callbacks for execution, with the polling channel serving as a fallback. Through the combination of real-time main loop, background periodic tasks, and push callbacks, robustness under network fluctuations can be improved while ensuring real-time performance, and the risk of the main loop being blocked by network operations is reduced.
408: This system adopts a three-tier collaborative architecture comprising device-side local recognition, cloud-side centralized management, and mobile-side remote control, with all parts working together to form a complete chain of visitor identity verification, visit trace recording, and remote handling. This chapter no longer discusses the design scheme itself, but rather focuses on three dimensions—three-tier closed loop, functionality and performance, and stability and security—to verify and analyze the system integration testing results.
409: 6.2 Three-Tier Integration Testing and Closed-Loop Verification
410: End-to-end integration testing is a critical link in system implementation, proceeding in three steps: first, establish the core interfaces (registration/login, device registration and heartbeat, visitor upload, list pagination, and statistics interfaces) to ensure the mobile side can see data; second, verify the stability of the device-side main link, focusing on whether consecutive frames cause repeated triggering and whether the camera freezes; third, handle occasional but real anomalies such as camera frame capture failure, network jitter, and acknowledgment loss, until the system can run stably over the long term.
411: Common problems during integration testing are mainly concentrated in three categories: field/structure inconsistencies causing client parsing failures; inconsistent image URL/static resource routing and return path specifications causing resource 404 errors; interface 500 errors caused by missing configurations, dependency version inconsistencies, and file directory permission issues. The solution is unified response encapsulation and error codes, with necessary compatibility on the client side.
412: The key to the remote control link lies in reachability and explainability. The system adopts MQTT topic subscription for receiving commands as the primary channel, supplemented by heartbeat polling as a fallback channel, to prevent commands from completely failing when MQTT is unavailable. The command state machine transforms remote control from a one-time request into a traceable process. The cloud maintains a status field for each command, simultaneously recording important time points such as created_at, delivered_at, and executed_at. After the device side reports the result, the cloud updates the status and saves the result.
413: For high-risk operations such as remote unlocking, it is recommended to default to rejecting execution when the device is offline or its status is unclear, with clear prompts explaining the reason on the client side. At the same time, use access_logs and remote_commands as audit evidence, ensuring every operation has a record for review.

433: Comprehensively considering functional testing, performance testing, and integration regression results, this system demonstrates usability in home doorstep scenarios: the recognition link and linkage actions are stable, visitor records can be completely traced and reviewed on the mobile side; the remote control closed loop has good reachability under the combined MQTT primary channel and HTTP polling fallback strategy, and forms an audit chain through command status and result reporting; cloud interfaces overall satisfy functional requirements and exhibit good response performance under indexing and pagination strategies.
434: Testing also revealed typical engineering issues and areas for improvement: edge-side FPS significantly decreases under high-resolution input, indicating that subsequent work still needs model lightweighting, quantization acceleration, or hardware acceleration to further improve real-time performance; interface return structures exhibited inconsistencies during early integration testing, suggesting that the server side needs to establish stricter interface specifications and automated testing; image upload and download under weak-network scenarios have a significant impact on experience, and more comprehensive breakpoint resumption and image compression strategies can be introduced subsequently. These conclusions provide clear directions for subsequent iteration.
438: This thesis, centered on the requirements of identity verification, visit trace recording, and remote handling in home doorstep scenarios, has completed the design and implementation of a Raspberry Pi based smart doorbell system with facial recognition. The system adopts a three-tier collaborative architecture of device-side local recognition, cloud-side centralized management, and mobile-side remote control, forming a complete link from recognition, recording, and reporting to remote command closed loop. On the device side, functions including real-time frame capture, face recognition, member admission and unlocking linkage, unknown visitor snapshot recording, and anomaly warning have been implemented, with stability enhanced through anti-duplicate triggering, self-recovery, and offline caching.
439: Comprehensively considering functional testing, performance observation, and integration regression results, the system demonstrates usability in home doorstep scenarios: the recognition link and linkage actions can run stably, visitor records can be traced and reviewed on the mobile side; the remote control closed loop has good reachability under the combined MQTT primary channel and heartbeat fallback strategy, and forms an audit chain through command status and result reporting. The above results verify the engineering feasibility of this thesis's approach and the foundation for further expansion.
440: Overall, this project has completed the full-link closed loop from edge recognition to cloud management to mobile-side control on a low-cost hardware platform, and has verified the system's operability under real network and environmental fluctuation conditions through integration and regression testing, laying a foundation for subsequent productization and functional expansion.
442: Subsequent improvements and expansions can be pursued in the following directions: (1) Algorithms and Performance: introduce more robust lightweight face detection/recognition models, perform quantization or hardware acceleration, and improve robustness under low light and complex poses; (2) Data and Experience: improve member multi-sample management, sample quality verification, and version synchronization mechanisms, and supplement push notifications, automatic Token refresh, and more user-friendly anomaly prompts; (3) Interaction Capability: add real-time video preview and richer doorstep interaction strategies to improve the remote monitoring experience.
